newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Australia cements low inflation reputation.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Australia cements low inflation reputation.

text.p: Australia's emerging reputation for being a low inflation country was bolstered on Wednesday by the release of inflation data showing consumer prices rising at their slowest rate in almost three years.
The consumer price index (CPI), or headline rate, rose 0.2 percent in the December quarter, to be 1.5 percent higher over the past year, slightly better than median expectations
The underlying rate, which is the focus of monetary policy, rose 0.4 percent in the quarter to be 2.1 percent higher over the past year, right on market expectations.

The annual rates of increase in the CPI and underlying measure of inflation were the lowest since the March 1994 and 1995 quarters respectively. The 0.2 percent rise in the December quarter CPI was the smallest quarterly rise since December 1993.

"Today's numbers continue the run of good outcomes which should be increasingly seen as a structural shift to low inflation rather than some temporary aberration," Commonwealth Bank senior economist Michael Blythe said.
Treasurer Costello also said that the data was consistent with the Reserve Bank of Australia's (RBA) objectives, and would contribute to an environment of low inflation.
The RBA targets the underlying inflation rate aiming to keep it to an average of two and three percent over a run of years.
The underlying rate excludes from the CPI seasonal and volatile items whose price movements are not mainly determined by demand forces, such as mortgage rate charges and government taxes and charges.

With some effects of the rise in the Australian dollar through 1996 still to be seen, and continued subdued growth in partial price indicators, inflation is expected to remain off the list of worries for economists through 1997.

"There are no obvious threats to near term inflation," Citibank Australia economists said in a commentary, adding that underlying inflation could fall to under 1.8 percent, the lowest level in the series' 25 year history, in the June quarter. While the outlook was for continued low inflation in 1997, economists said the data did not mean that interest rates would be lowered following next week's RBA board meeting.

Low inflation was a necessary, but not sufficient, condition for lower interest rates. Wages, and possibly developments U.S. interest rates, would determine whether or not there is another cut in the official cash rate.
Societe Generale chief economist John Edwards said that while there was room for a rate cut on price grounds, and probably on activty grounds as well, he was not expecting one next week.

"With three cuts behind it, the RBA is now likely to wait and see both the December quarter average weekly earnings numbers next week, and the Industrial Relations Commission on the ACTU (Australian Council of Trade Unions) "Living Wage" claim in February or March," he said.
